title: Who do you say I am (Mark 8:27–38)
word: Who do you say I am
hook: Peter gets the answer right and the meaning wrong

segments.voice: Yesterday, men as trees: a blind man healed in two stages, blurry first, then clear. Your line was healing in stages. What stage did you name? Today, Peter sees half of it. Day two hundred fourteen.

Everyone has had a friend ask, what do people say about me? It's a nervous question, usually. Today Jesus asks it, and he isn't nervous. He's walking with his disciples on the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, far north, near the springs where the Jordan begins, in a town named after an emperor. And he asks: who do people say I am? The answers come fast. John the Baptist, back from the dead. Elijah. One of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide from it.
screen: `WHAT DO PEOPLE SAY ABOUT ME?` → `CAESAREA PHILIPPI, FAR NORTH.` → `JOHN, ELIJAH, A PROPHET.`

segments.voice: First, the right answer. In the Douay-Rheims: "But whom do you say that I am? Peter answering said to him: Thou art the Christ." Christ isn't a last name. It's the Greek for anointed, the same as the Hebrew word Messiah. Kings were anointed with oil. For many in Israel, the Messiah meant the king God would send to set his people free. This is the hinge of Mark's Gospel: halfway through, someone finally says it out loud. Second, the wrong meaning. Right away Jesus starts teaching that the Son of man must suffer many things, be rejected, be killed, and rise again after three days. Mark says he spoke openly. And Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. Messiahs don't die. That's not the plan. Third, the rebuke back, the hardest words Jesus says to a friend: "Go behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but that are of men." Many readers notice the first two words. Go behind me. It's where a disciple walks. Peter has stepped in front, trying to lead, and Jesus sends him back to his place. Fourth, the invitation to everyone. Jesus calls the crowd over too: "If any man will follow me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." In Rome's world a cross wasn't jewelry. It was how the empire executed rebels and slaves, in public. Nobody hearing this thought it was a metaphor for a small annoyance. Catholics read it as the shape of the whole Christian life: not a grim road, but following someone who walked it first.
screen: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.` · `THE SON OF MAN MUST SUFFER.` · `GO BEHIND ME: A DISCIPLE'S PLACE.` · `TAKE UP YOUR CROSS AND FOLLOW.` · then, large: `WHOM DO YOU SAY THAT I AM?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer the question in one sentence. Settle and breathe. Imagine the road, the dust, and the question turned toward you. Not what the Church says. Not what your parents said. Who do you say he is? Maybe the answer is sure. Maybe it's I don't know yet. Maybe it's a question back. Any honest sentence counts. Say it quietly, once. Then sit with it. If you pray, you can offer that sentence as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Who do you say I am. The question Jesus asks his disciples at Caesarea Philippi, halfway through Mark, and the question the whole Gospel turns on. Today's word.
screen: `WHO DO YOU SAY I AM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: take up your cross. Today, carry one hard thing without complaining about it out loud, and walk behind someone instead of in front. Day two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Catholics profess who Jesus is each Sunday in the Creed, and many speak of daily hardships as crosses carried with Christ, sometimes offering them up in prayer.

original.note: Greek: cross, the Roman stake of execution. take up your cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter, the star pupil, gets it right.
what it means: Peter names him the Christ, then refuses the suffering. he's sent back behind, to follow.
what a scholar hears: the hinge of Mark, at Caesarea Philippi, followed by the first of three predictions of the passion.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 8:29, 8:33 and 8:34 given from memory; confirm (8:29 opens 'Then he saith to them' in Challoner; only the words from 'But whom' are quoted).
Caesarea Philippi described as near the springs of the Jordan and named after an emperor (Caesar Augustus / Tiberius, by Philip the tetrarch); confirm.
The 'go behind me = the disciple's place' reading (Greek opisō mou, as in 1:17 and 8:34) is presented as what many readers notice; confirm.
The index title is 'Who do you say I am'; the Douay reads 'whom do you say that I am'. Kept both.
